title: OPRA Long-Term Results: Watch-and-Wait After Total Neoadjuvant Therapy for Rectal Cancer
breakthrough: The randomised phase II OPRA trial's long-term analysis followed 324 patients with locally advanced rectal cancer through a median 5.1 years after total neoadjuvant therapy, comparing induction chemotherapy then chemoradiation against chemoradiation then consolidation chemotherapy, with non-operative watch-and-wait offered to complete and near-complete responders. Five-year disease-free survival was 71% and 69% respectively (P=.68), while TME-free survival — organ preservation — was 39% versus 54% (P=.012), favouring consolidation chemotherapy. Critically, disease-free survival was identical, 64% versus 64% (P=.94), whether a patient went straight to total mesorectal excision after restaging or entered watch-and-wait and had salvage TME for regrowth.
impact: Roughly half of patients keep their rectum without paying for it in disease-free survival, and the sequence of the neoadjuvant regimen — not just its components — determines how many. NCCN and ASCRS now list non-operative management as an option for complete clinical responders discussed in a multidisciplinary setting.
practical: Watch-and-wait is a surveillance commitment, not the absence of treatment: of 81 regrowths, 94% appeared within two years and 99% within three, so the schedule is intensive early — endoscopy and MRI at short intervals for the first two years. Salvage TME preserved outcomes only because regrowth was caught while still resectable. Select for it where surveillance is deliverable and the patient will attend; a complete clinical response is not a cure, and the trade being offered is avoiding a permanent stoma and low anterior resection syndrome in exchange for years of scans.
link: OPRA long-term results — organ preservation after total neoadjuvant therapy in rectal adenocarcinoma

verify.status: NOT FOUND — the submitted trial name belongs to an unrelated study; replaced with the real evidence base
verify.note: The submission titled this entry 'Phase III SUNLIGHT Trial: Watch-and-Wait vs. Total Mesorectal Excision'. SUNLIGHT is a real phase III trial, but it is trifluridine/tipiracil plus bevacizumab versus trifluridine/tipiracil alone in refractory METASTATIC colorectal cancer (492 patients, median OS 10.8 vs 7.5 months, HR 0.61) — it has nothing to do with watch-and-wait, rectal cancer or surgery. No Lancet randomised trial of watch-and-wait versus TME could be found; a randomised comparison of the two has never been done and probably cannot be, since randomising a complete responder to surgery has failed to recruit. The actual evidence base is the randomised phase II OPRA trial (long-term results, JCO 2023/2025 analyses) plus the International Watch & Wait Database registry, and the surviving-equal-survival claim is supported specifically by OPRA's 64% vs 64% DFS for planned TME versus salvage TME after regrowth. Entry rewritten to that evidence, with the surveillance burden and regrowth timing added. NOTE: trifluridine/tipiracil has now appeared TWICE in this review as a wrong-drug/wrong-trial title (previously in the ophthalmology list, for ocular surface squamous neoplasia) — worth watching as a recurring source of contamination.

title: DIRECT Trial: Robotic Versus Laparoscopic TAPP Inguinal Hernia Repair
breakthrough: The Danish Inguinal Randomized Controlled Trial (DIRECT) randomised 138 patients to robot-assisted (n=74) or laparoscopic (n=64) transabdominal preperitoneal repair by experienced surgeons. Time from intubation to skin closure and from insufflation to instrument removal were both shorter for the robotic approach, with a larger difference for complicated defects. Pooled against the other randomised evidence — a meta-analysis of three RCTs totalling 300 patients — robotic repair showed a longer operative time that did not reach significance and no significant difference in complication rates.
impact: The randomised evidence for robotic TAPP is thin — three trials, 300 patients — and it does not yet show an outcome advantage over laparoscopy. What it does show is that in experienced hands the robot is not slower, which is the opposite of the usual objection.
practical: Treat robotic TAPP as an equivalent option chosen for surgeon ergonomics and case complexity, not as an upgrade you can promise a patient. Nothing randomised supports a chronic-pain or conversion advantage in complex, incarcerated or post-radiation groin defects, and HerniaSurge/SAGES have not defined anatomical criteria mandating the robot. The cost differential is real and the outcome differential is not established, so a unit adopting it should be auditing its own conversion and chronic pain rates rather than assuming the benefit.
link: DIRECT — shorter operative times following robotic-assisted TAPP compared with laparoscopic TAPP

verify.status: NOT FOUND — trial name unresolvable, and the submitted findings are REVERSED against the randomised evidence
verify.note: No trial named 'COLA-TAPP' exists in the searchable literature, and no JAMA Surgery randomised trial of robotic versus laparoscopic TAPP could be found. The submission's specific claims — that robotic TAPP 'significantly lowers 30-day chronic pain rates and operative conversion in complex, incarcerated, or post-radiation groin defects' and that HerniaSurge/SAGES have been updated to define anatomical criteria for robot use — are not supported: the 2025 meta-analysis of three RCTs (300 patients) found no significant difference in complications and a non-significant TREND toward LONGER robotic operative time. The real randomised trial in this space is DIRECT (Hernia 2025, 138 patients), whose finding is about operative time, not pain. Entry rewritten to DIRECT plus the meta-analysis, with the unsupported outcome claims removed and the cost caveat kept.

title: MERLIN_001: Gene Expression Profiling to Omit Sentinel Node Biopsy in Melanoma
breakthrough: A nine-centre prospective study applied the CP-GEP test — clinicopathological factors combined with an eight-gene expression profile — in a blinded fashion to 1,761 patients with primary cutaneous melanoma who underwent sentinel lymph node biopsy per current guidelines. It is the largest study of a melanoma gene test performed. CP-GEP stratified T1–T3 melanomas into risk groups with a three-fold separation in sentinel node positivity: 23.8% in the high-risk group against 7.1% in the low-risk group, giving a negative predictive value of 92.9%.
impact: NCCN Cutaneous Melanoma guidelines version 1.2026 name CP-GEP as the first and only molecular test that may be used to inform the sentinel node biopsy decision in selected early-stage patients. Sentinel node biopsy is a staging operation with real morbidity and no demonstrated melanoma-specific survival benefit, so a test that identifies who can skip it changes the consent conversation rather than the cancer treatment.
practical: The number that matters is the 7.1% residual risk in the low-risk group, not the 92.9% NPV — they are the same number stated two ways, and the patient hears them differently. Roughly a third of surgical candidates fall into the low-risk group. Position this as shared decision-making: a low-risk result does not exclude nodal disease, and sentinel node status still carries prognostic weight and gates access to adjuvant therapy trials. It is a commercial assay (SkylineDx), so confirm it is covered before promising it.
link: MERLIN_001 — gene expression profile–based test to predict melanoma sentinel node status

verify.status: matched — verified, with the risk framing restored
verify.note: Verified in full: MERLIN_001, JAMA Surgery October 2025, 1,761 patients, largest melanoma gene-test study, high-risk 23.8% versus low-risk 7.1% sentinel node positivity, NCCN Cutaneous Melanoma v1.2026 recognition. The submission's 92.9% NPV and 'less than 10% risk' are internally consistent with the published 7.1% — 92.9% NPV IS the 7.1% metastasis rate, so nothing was overstated. Two additions: the submission's 'nearly 37% of surgical candidates' spared is plausible but not confirmed in the accessible sources, so it is softened to 'roughly a third'; and the source material's own framing — that SLNB has prognostic value but no universal melanoma-specific survival benefit, so this is for shared decision-making — has been restored, because the submission presented the result as approval to forgo the operation. SSO guideline endorsement could not be confirmed; only NCCN is asserted.

title: PREPARE Pilot Trial: Preoperative Beta-Lactam Allergy Delabelling by Direct Oral Challenge
breakthrough: The PREPARE pilot randomised clinical trial enrolled 150 adults across three tertiary hospitals in Melbourne who reported a beta-lactam allergy and were likely to need intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis for surgery. An anaesthesiologist-led preoperative clinic used a smartphone decision-support algorithm to risk-stratify; of the 28 classified low risk, 93% were successfully delabelled by direct oral challenge. There were no severe adverse events and no surgical delays.
impact: Reported penicillin allergy is wrong in the great majority of cases, and the label costs the patient first-line cefazolin prophylaxis. This shows the delabelling can be done inside the existing preoperative workup rather than requiring an allergy referral and skin testing — building on PALACE (JAMA Internal Medicine 2023), which established that direct oral challenge is non-inferior to skin testing followed by oral challenge in low-risk patients.
practical: Note the denominator: only 28 of 150 patients were low risk, so this is not a universal screen — it is a pathway for the subset whose history is clearly low risk, and the risk stratification is the hard part. This is a PILOT trial designed for feasibility and safety, not powered for clinical outcomes: it did not measure surgical site infection or C. difficile rates, so the downstream benefit is inferred from cefazolin's known superiority as prophylaxis, not demonstrated here. Do not run direct oral challenges without the risk-stratification tool and resuscitation capability in place.
link: PREPARE — perioperative penicillin and cephalosporin antibiotic allergy assessment and testing pilot RCT

verify.status: corrected — real trial, but design and outcomes were overstated
verify.note: The study is real: PREPARE pilot RCT, JAMA Surgery 26 March 2025, 150 patients, three Melbourne hospitals. Four corrections. (1) The submission calls it a 'Phase II multi-center randomized clinical trial'; it is a PILOT trial — feasibility and safety, not powered for clinical endpoints. (2) 'anesthesiologist- and surgeon-led' — the published intervention is anaesthesiologist-led. (3) The submission states the trial 'directly reduc[es] Surgical Site Infections (SSIs) and C. difficile rates'; those outcomes were not measured, and presenting an inference as a trial result is the error class this review keeps finding. (4) The submission omits that only 28 of 150 enrolled patients were low risk and eligible for direct oral challenge, which is the number that determines how much of a surgical list this actually applies to. PALACE added as the RCT that underpins the non-inferiority claim. No SIS or ASA guideline change to this effect could be found; the guideline sentence has been removed.

title: Drains After Pancreatoduodenectomy: Selective Early Removal, Not Omission
journal: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews / HPB
breakthrough: The 2025 Cochrane review and a companion meta-analysis of five randomised trials totalling 1,337 patients found no significant difference in morbidity, major morbidity, intra-abdominal abscess, wound infection, haemorrhage or reintervention between drain and no-drain policies overall, with the evidence for 90-day mortality rated very uncertain. The synthesised recommendation splits by operation: a selective EARLY DRAIN REMOVAL policy for pancreatoduodenectomy, and a no-drain policy for left (distal) pancreatectomy. PANDORINA, the binational RCT that stratifies by fistula risk, is the trial designed to settle the high-risk question.
impact: The field has converged on when to take the drain out rather than whether to place one. Early removal — around postoperative day 3 in patients whose day-1 drain amylase is low — reduces complications without the risk of having no access to an undrained leak.
practical: Do not read this as licence to omit drains in a high-risk pancreatoduodenectomy. The multicentre RCT of PD with versus without routine intraperitoneal drainage (Van Buren, Annals of Surgery 2014) was STOPPED EARLY by its data safety monitoring board because mortality rose from 3% to 12% in the no-drain arm, with more frequent and more severe complications. A soft gland and a small duct are precisely the setting in which that trial's harm signal appeared. Place the drain, check day-1 amylase, and pull it on day 3 if the number is low — that is the evidence-supported sequence.
link: Cochrane — prophylactic abdominal drainage for pancreatic surgery (2025 update)

verify.status: REVERSED — the submission's safety conclusion is the opposite of the randomised evidence in the highest-risk group
verify.note: SAFETY-RELEVANT. The submission described a 'landmark international randomized trial published in Annals of Surgery' evaluating early drain removal versus NO prophylactic drain in patients with soft pancreatic texture or small duct — i.e. exactly the high-risk group — and concluded that 'routine prophylactic drain placement in high-risk anastomoses does not prevent Grade C postoperative pancreatic fistulas'. No such trial could be found, and the direction is wrong: the randomised multi-institutional trial of PD with versus without routine intraperitoneal drainage (Van Buren et al., Annals of Surgery 2014) was TERMINATED EARLY by its DSMB because mortality increased from 3% to 12% without drains, concluding that routine elimination of drains in PD increases mortality and the severity and frequency of complications. A trainee reading the submitted entry could omit a drain in a soft-gland Whipple on the belief that a trial showed it safe. The genuine 2025 evidence — Cochrane CD010583.pub6 and the five-RCT meta-analysis (1,337 patients) — supports SELECTIVE EARLY REMOVAL for pancreatoduodenectomy and no-drain only for left pancreatectomy; PANDORINA is the risk-stratified trial in progress. Entry rewritten with the Van Buren harm signal stated explicitly. The submission's day-3 early-removal point is retained because it is correct and supported.

title: IntAct: ICG Fluorescence Angiography Did Not Significantly Reduce Anastomotic Leak
breakthrough: IntAct, an unblinded randomised controlled trial at 28 specialist rectal cancer centres in eight European countries, assigned 766 patients to intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence angiography or standard perfusion assessment. Clinical anastomotic leak within 90 days occurred in 36 of 343 (10%) with ICG versus 54 of 355 (15%) with standard care — adjusted odds ratio 0.667, 95% CI 0.419–1.060, p=0.087. The result did not reach significance. Grade C leak rates were similar between groups, so any benefit sits in grade A/B leaks.
impact: This is the largest randomised test of a technique already in wide use, and it is negative on its primary endpoint. The AVOID trial in minimally invasive colorectal surgery reached a comparable conclusion. The direction of effect is favourable and the trial may simply be underpowered for a 5-percentage-point difference, but the honest statement is that ICG is not proven to prevent clinically significant leaks.
practical: ICG remains reasonable to use — it is cheap, quick and safe, and the signal points the right way — but it should not be presented to a patient or a trainee as an established leak-prevention measure, and it must not substitute for the things that are established: tension-free anastomosis, adequate proximal division, splenic flexure mobilisation where needed, and a diverting stoma when the anastomosis is low and the patient is high risk. Assessment is not standardised across centres, which is the leading candidate explanation for the null result and the reason quantitative protocols are the current research focus.
link: IntAct — intraoperative fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green to prevent anastomotic leak in rectal cancer surgery

verify.status: REVERSED — the submission reports a significant reduction; the landmark RCT was not significant
verify.note: The submission stated ICG 'significantly lowers anastomotic leak rates' and that ASCRS and EAES have issued consensus statements endorsing quantitative ICG perfusion mapping as a standard intraoperative safety tool. Both are wrong. IntAct (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology 2025, 766 randomised patients, 28 centres, 8 countries) found 10% versus 15% clinical leak, adjusted OR 0.667, p=0.087 — NOT significant; the authors' own interpretation is that a signal was observed and future research must standardise ICG assessment. The AVOID phase 3 trial reached a similar conclusion. No ASCRS or EAES consensus establishing ICG as a standard safety tool could be found. The submitted journal was also wrong: British Journal of Surgery, not Lancet Gastro Hep. Entry rewritten to the actual result, keeping the favourable direction and the standardisation problem, and adding what a trainee should NOT stop doing on the strength of a fluorescence image.

title: Antibiotics Versus Appendectomy for Uncomplicated Appendicitis: Long-Term Outcomes
journal: New England Journal of Medicine / JAMA Surgery
breakthrough: Long-term follow-up of the two major randomised trials now quantifies what antibiotics-first buys. In CODA (NEJM), about half of patients assigned to antibiotics had not undergone appendectomy by four years; the trial deliberately included patients with an appendicolith or perforation, which drove its appendectomy rate above earlier work. In APPAC, which excluded those patients, the five-year appendectomy rate in the antibiotics arm was 39% — 61% appendectomy-free. WSES and ACS guidance treats antibiotics as a legitimate definitive option with shared decision-making.
impact: The conversation is now quantitative: roughly half to three-fifths of patients avoid an operation, and the difference between the two trials is patient selection — an appendicolith substantially raises the chance antibiotics fail.
practical: One thing the submission got backwards and that matters clinically: non-operative management means the appendix is never examined histologically, so an occult appendiceal neoplasm is NOT excluded — it is left undiagnosed. Incidental neoplasms are found in roughly 1% of appendectomy specimens and more often over age 40, which is an argument for appendectomy or for interval imaging in older patients, not a reassurance. Screen out the appendicolith, set the expectation of a real recurrence rate before discharge, and make sure the patient knows what to come back for.
link: CODA — antibiotics versus appendectomy for acute appendicitis, longer-term outcomes

verify.status: corrected — figure overstated and the neoplasm reassurance is REVERSED
verify.note: Three corrections. (1) The submission claims 'over 65% of patients treated initially with antibiotics remain successfully appendectomy-free at 5 years'. The published figures are lower: CODA's NEJM longer-term report is at FOUR years with about half avoiding appendectomy, and APPAC's five-year appendectomy-free rate is 61%. No source supports over 65% at five years. (2) The submission asserts no increased risk of 'occult appendiceal neoplasm' — this is backwards. Non-operative management removes the histological specimen from the pathway, so occult neoplasms are not excluded but simply not looked for; this is a recognised concern with antibiotics-first, particularly over age 40, and it has been restored as a caution. (3) The entry is framed as a single 5-year NEJM publication; the evidence is two trials with different inclusion criteria (CODA included appendicolith and perforation, APPAC did not), and that difference is the reason their numbers diverge, so both are now named.

title: Endoscopic Versus Surgical Step-Up for Infected Necrotising Pancreatitis
breakthrough: The Dutch multicentre randomised superiority trial across 19 hospitals assigned adults with infected necrotising pancreatitis to an endoscopic step-up approach — EUS-guided transluminal drainage, then endoscopic necrosectomy if needed — or a surgical step-up approach of percutaneous catheter drainage then video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement. The composite primary endpoint of major complications or death at six months was NOT different between the groups. Endoscopic step-up did produce a shorter hospital stay and significantly fewer pancreatic fistulas. Lumen-apposing metal stents have since largely replaced plastic stents for the drainage step.
impact: Endoscopy-first is preferred where expertise exists — but for stay and fistula, not survival. APA/IAP and subsequent guidance position it as the favoured route while retaining the step-up principle itself, which remains the important lesson: drain first, debride only if drainage fails.
practical: The choice is driven by anatomy and available expertise. Endoscopic drainage needs a collection abutting the stomach or duodenum and an interventional endoscopist; retroperitoneal collections without a luminal window still go percutaneous or surgical. Do not promise a mortality or organ-failure benefit — the trial did not show one. LAMS carry their own complications, chiefly bleeding from an eroded vessel and buried-stent syndrome, so removal timing needs a plan at insertion.
link: TENSION — endoscopic or surgical step-up approach for infected necrotising pancreatitis: a multicentre randomised trial

verify.status: corrected — organ-failure benefit REVERSED, journal citation conflated two journals, date wrong by eight years
verify.note: The submission described a 'multi-center randomized trial published in Gastroenterology & Annals of Surgery' comparing LAMS endoscopic step-up against minimally invasive surgical necrosectomy, and claimed it 'dramatically reduces systemic inflammatory stress, MAJOR ORGAN FAILURE RATES, post-procedural pancreatic fistulas, and overall hospital length of stay'. The organ-failure claim is REVERSED: the defining trial (TENSION, Lancet 2017, 19 Dutch hospitals) found NO difference in its composite of major complications or death; the benefits were shorter stay and fewer pancreatic fistulas. 'Gastroenterology & Annals of Surgery' conflates two separate journals into one citation — the same error pattern as the ophthalmology list's 'Gastroenterology & Radiology'. The trial is 2017, not a 2025 development, and no 2025 randomised LAMS-versus-surgery trial could be found. Entry rewritten with the correct result and the anatomical/expertise constraints and LAMS-specific complications added; the step-up principle and the fistula/stay benefit are retained because they are real.

title: Prehospital Resuscitative Thoracotomy for Traumatic Cardiac Arrest
breakthrough: A retrospective cohort study reviewed every prehospital resuscitative thoracotomy performed for out-of-hospital traumatic cardiac arrest by London's physician-led prehospital service from 1999 to 2019 — 601 patients. Five per cent survived to hospital discharge; 73.4% of those who did not were pronounced dead at the scene. Underlying causes were exsanguination in 70%, cardiac tamponade in 17.6%, and both in 12.1%. Survival was concentrated in the tamponade group.
impact: Twenty years of data establish that the procedure is feasible in a mature physician-staffed urban prehospital system and that it salvages a small number of patients who would otherwise die at the scene — most clearly when the mechanism is tamponade and no other option exists.
practical: Five per cent overall survival is the number to carry, and it comes from a service with on-scene physicians, short urban transport times and two decades of accumulated practice — it does not transfer to a paramedic-only system or a rural one. Selection is the whole procedure: penetrating chest injury with witnessed loss of vital signs and suspected tamponade is the group with something to gain; blunt arrest and prolonged downtime are not. EAST and ACS-COT guidance on point-of-injury surgical resuscitation should be read for the criteria rather than inferred from the headline.
link: Prehospital resuscitative thoracotomy for traumatic cardiac arrest

verify.status: corrected — study design misstated and the comparative claim does not exist in the paper
verify.note: The paper is real: Perkins et al., JAMA Surgery, published online 26 February 2025. Two corrections, both about what it can support. (1) The submission calls it 'a high-impact trial' that 'evaluated survival and neurological outcomes following physician-led prehospital resuscitative thoracotomy versus standard emergency department thoracotomy'. It is a RETROSPECTIVE COHORT of 601 London cases over 21 years with NO comparison group — there is no versus. (2) It therefore cannot and does not 'prove that executing immediate thoracotomy at the scene significantly improves neurologically intact survival compared to delayed in-hospital thoracotomy'; that comparison was never made. The published survival is 5% to hospital discharge, which the submission omitted entirely, and the benefit signal is specific to cardiac tamponade. Entry rewritten to the cohort's actual findings with the causes breakdown and the system-dependence caveat added, since a 5% figure from a physician-staffed urban service is not portable.

title: De-Escalation of Nodal Surgery in Clinically Node-Positive Breast Cancer
breakthrough: A cohort study evaluated oncologic outcomes of de-escalating axillary surgery in patients with clinically node-positive breast cancer who converted to clinically node-negative after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, comparing targeted axillary dissection — retrieval of a clipped, biopsy-proven metastatic node alongside standard sentinel nodes — against completion axillary lymph node dissection. Targeted axillary dissection enabled safe de-escalation in patients with low-volume residual disease, with localisation improving clipped-node retrieval, while completion axillary clearance carried higher morbidity.
impact: Targeted axillary dissection has moved from a technique for reducing false-negative rates to the basis for omitting axillary clearance in selected patients, and SSO/ASCO practice has shifted with it. Lymphoedema, shoulder dysfunction and chronic pain after full clearance are the morbidity this avoids.
practical: "Low-volume residual disease" is doing the work in that sentence, and where the line sits is not settled. Alliance A011202 — the randomised phase III trial comparing completion axillary dissection to axillary radiation in patients with a positive sentinel node after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — closed to randomisation in 2022 and its correlative analyses show why the question is live: among patients with ypN1mi disease, 38.4% had additional positive nodes found at completion dissection. Clip the biopsied node at diagnosis; without it targeted axillary dissection is not available later. Confirm the clipped node was actually retrieved before calling the axilla staged.
link: De-escalation of nodal surgery in clinically node-positive breast cancer

verify.status: unresolved on specifics — the study and direction are confirmed, the cohort size is not
verify.note: Confirmed: a JAMA Surgery cohort study on de-escalation of nodal surgery in clinically node-positive breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy exists, and its conclusion — targeted axillary dissection permits safe de-escalation in low-volume residual disease, completion clearance carries higher morbidity, localisation improves clipped-node retrieval — matches the submission's direction. Three things could NOT be confirmed and have been removed or softened: the '976 patients' figure, the '5-year regional recurrence' framing (this is a cohort study, and the accessible sources do not state a five-year recurrence endpoint), and the claim that the study is prospective. Added: it is a cohort study, not randomised, and Alliance A011202 is the trial that will settle the question — its reported correlative finding that 38.4% of ypN1mi patients had additional positive nodes at completion dissection is the concrete reason 'low-volume' needs definition. Added the practical prerequisite the submission omitted: the node must be clipped at diagnostic biopsy or targeted axillary dissection is impossible.
